title: HF Sync & AI Feedback Setup for Topic 1 Questions
text:
This document explains how the GitHub Actions workflow syncs topic1questions content to Hugging Face Space and integrates it with the AI feedback system in app.py.






Added Pre-Sync Quarto Render Step:
- name: Set up Quarto (for rendering topic1questions)
  uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
- name: Render topic1questions.qmd to HTML
  run: |
    quarto render topic1questions.qmd --to html
Why? - Ensures fresh HTML: Every time you push to GitHub, the workflow automatically renders topic1questions.qmd → docs/topic1questions.html - No manual render needed: You forget to render locally before pushing? No problem—GitHub does it for you - Syncs both source & rendered: Both topic1questions.qmd (source) and docs/topic1questions.html (rendered) go to HF Space
Files Synced to HF Space (Lean): - app.py — Shiny app (AI feedback engine) - shared.py — Helper functions - requirements.txt — Dependencies - Dockerfile — Container config - README.hf.md → README.md — Instructions - topic1questions.qmd — Source file (for reference) - docs/topic1questions.html — Rendered HTML (for viewing/context)
Files NOT Synced (Large, stay on GitHub only): - ppt/ folder (all PPTX + PNG) - docs/ images - Anything else not explicitly copied




You push to main branch on GitHub
GitHub Actions triggers automatically
Workflow renders topic1questions.qmd → docs/topic1questions.html
Workflow copies lean files (app, config, topic1 content) to HF Space
HF Space updates with fresh content
AI feedback app on HF Space has access to question context








Load Questions from QMD (Optional Context):
def load_questions_from_qmd():
    """Load question text from topic1questions.qmd for better context."""
    qmd_path = pathlib.Path("topic1questions.qmd")
    if qmd_path.exists():
        try:
            content = qmd_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
            return content
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Warning: Could not load topic1questions.qmd: {e}")
    return None
Enhanced Feedback Prompt: - The create_feedback_prompt() now calls load_questions_from_qmd() - If topic1questions.qmd exists (on HF Space), the AI tutor has access to the full source for richer context - Falls back gracefully if file is missing
Updated UI: - Title: “Week 1 Tutorial Questions” → “Topic 1 - Monetary Economics Questions” - Added links to topic1questions.qmd and docs/topic1questions.html in the instructions




Context-Aware: AI tutor can reference the original question file for more nuanced guidance
Consistency: Same questions on GitHub → HF Space → AI feedback system
Decoupled: Questions are not hardcoded in Python; they live in QMD files and are loaded dynamically








A “pre-sync render” means: before uploading to HF Space, render all QMD files to HTML locally (in GitHub Actions).
- name: Set up Quarto (for rendering topic1questions)
  uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
- name: Render topic1questions.qmd to HTML
  run: |
    quarto render topic1questions.qmd --to html






Without Pre-Sync Render
With Pre-Sync Render




HF Space gets old/stale HTML
Fresh HTML synced every push


Manual render step easy to forget
Automatic, never forgotten


docs/topic1questions.html might be out of sync
Always up-to-date







Time: Adds ~30-60 seconds to workflow (rendering QMD → HTML)
Benefit: Guaranteed fresh content on HF Space; no manual steps




To add more topics later (e.g., topic2questions, topic3questions):
- name: Render all questions to HTML
  run: |
    quarto render topic1questions.qmd --to html
    quarto render topic2questions.qmd --to html
    quarto render topic3questions.qmd --to html
Then update the sync section to copy all rendered files:
cp docs/topic*.html "${WORKDIR}/docs/" 2>/dev/null || true





┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ You push to GitHub (main branch)        │
└────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ GitHub Actions Triggered                │
│ 1. Set up Quarto                        │
│ 2. Render topic1questions.qmd → HTML    │
│ 3. Copy lean files                      │
│ 4. Push to HF Space                     │
└────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HF Space Updated                        │
│ - app.py ready to serve                 │
│ - topic1questions.qmd & HTML available  │
│ - AI feedback system has context        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘




After updating the workflow, test by:

Push a small change to GitHub:
git add .
git commit -m "Test HF sync workflow"
git push origin main
Check GitHub Actions:

Go to your repo → “Actions” tab
Watch the “Sync HF Space” workflow run
Should complete in 1-2 minutes

Verify on HF Space:

Open your HF Space: https://huggingface.co/spaces/camcalderon777/monetary-economics-topic1-questions
Check that the app loads
Check files in the HF Space repo (should see topic1questions.qmd, docs/topic1questions.html)







Add topic2questions, topic3questions, etc. following the same pattern
Render all topicXquestions.qmd files in a loop (don’t repeat yourself)
Consider adding a CI check: fail the workflow if Quarto render fails (to catch errors early)
Optional: cache Quarto rendering to speed up workflow






.github/workflows/hf-space-sync.yml — Updated with pre-sync render + topic1 content sync
app.py — Updated to load topic1questions.qmd dynamically and enhance feedback prompt
README.md (this file) — Documentation

Done! The setup is now lean, automatic, and scalable.

title: Topic 1 - MCQs Formative Assessment
text:
How to use this quiz



This quiz is designed as a formative self-assessment tool, not as a test.
Its purpose is to help you: - check your understanding of the key concepts from Topic 1, - identify which types of thinking you find more difficult, and - guide your revision before the tutorial and future assessments.


Each question belongs to one of four categories:

Subject Knowledge (SK): definitions, concepts, and facts.

Analysis (AN): understanding relationships and economic mechanisms.

Problem Solving (PS): applying concepts to new situations.

Mathematical Thinking (MT): working with ratios, prices, and scaling.

Your score will be broken down by category so you can see where you are strong and where you need more practice.




You may use your notes and the lecture materials.
Take your time — the goal is understanding, not speed.
Use the Hints if you get stuck.
You may refresh and retry the quiz as many times as you like.





A low score is not a problem — it tells you what to focus on.
If you score low in:

SK: revise definitions and core concepts.
AN: revisit the logic of the models and examples.
PS: practise applying concepts to new cases.
MT: practise the price and ratio calculations.





The leaderboard is optional and anonymous. It exists only to make practice more engaging.
It has no effect on your grade and is not used for evaluation.
The only purpose of this quiz is to support your learning.
crumbs: Topic 1 - The Nature and Economic Role of Money

title: Topic 1 - MCQs Formative Assessment
text:
Subject Knowledge

SK1) Which of the following is not one of the three economic roles of money?


 Medium of exchange Unit of account Store of value Means of production




Hint

The three roles concern valuation, exchange, and storage — not production activities.



SK2) Which role of money refers to its function as a generally accepted means of payment?


 Unit of account Medium of exchange Store of value Liquidity provider




Hint

The role that enables buying and selling is the Medium of Exchange.



SK3) Which role of money allows prices to be expressed and compared across goods?


 Store of value Medium of exchange Unit of account Asset




Hint

Prices can be compared only if money acts as a common measurement unit.



SK4) Which of the following best defines liquidity?


 The legal tender status of an asset The ease with which an asset can be exchanged for goods or other assets The interest paid by an asset The stability of an asset's price over time




Hint

Liquidity refers to how easily an asset can be exchanged, not to its return or price stability.



SK5) Which monetary aggregate is conventionally defined as “money” in modern economies?


 M0 M1 M2 M3




Hint

The conventional definition includes assets that can be used directly for payment.



SK6) Which of the following is not one of the four characteristics that underlie liquidity?


 Marketability Predictability of exchange value Divisibility Scarcity




Hint

Scarcity affects value, not the ease with which an asset can be exchanged.



SK7) Which of the following best explains why money is considered “intrinsically worthless” in modern economies?


 It has no legal status It is not backed by gold It has no direct consumption or production use It is issued by private banks




Hint

“Intrinsically worthless” means money has no direct consumption or production use.



SK8) Which of the following objects is an example of a Unit of Account that is not a Medium of Exchange?


 Euro banknotes Bitcoin IMF Special Drawing Rights (SDR) Gold




Hint

Some units exist only for accounting and pricing, not for everyday transactions.



SK9) Why does money’s role as a Store of Value logically follow from its role as a Medium of Exchange?


 Because money is durable Because money is scarce Because there is typically a time gap between selling and buying Because money earns interest




Hint

Because selling and buying are separated in time, money must store value between them.



SK10) Which statement best reflects the Classical view of money?


 Money directly affects real output Money is a veil over real economic activity Money determines the level of employment Money is essential for price formation




Hint

The Classical view treats money as neutral with respect to real economic outcomes.
crumbs: Topic 1 - The Nature and Economic Role of Money

title: Topic 1 - MCQs Formative Assessment
text:
Analysis

AN1) Why does barter require a “double coincidence of wants”?


 Because goods are indivisible Because both traders must want what the other offers Because prices cannot be defined Because barter requires legal contracts




Hint

Trade requires that each party wants what the other offers at the same time.



AN2) Why does the use of money reduce search costs relative to barter?


 Because prices become regulated Because money replaces goods Because traders only need to find someone who accepts money Because money increases production




Hint

With money, traders only need to find someone who accepts money, not a specific good.



AN3) Why does the existence of a Unit of Account reduce the informational burden in an economy?


 It eliminates uncertainty It reduces the number of relative prices that must be known It stabilises inflation It ensures fairness in trade




Hint

A Unit of Account reduces the number of prices that must be known and compared.



AN4) Why does money’s liquidity allow people to accept a lower financial return on it?


 Because money is scarce Because money is safe Because liquidity provides convenience and flexibility Because money is legally protected




Hint

People accept lower returns because liquidity itself is valuable.



AN5) Why does the Classical view regard money as a “veil”?


 Because money hides inequality Because money only affects nominal variables, not real outcomes Because money is unstable Because money is controlled by governments




Hint

The Classical view separates nominal prices from real economic outcomes.



AN6) Why does Keynes argue that money has macroeconomic importance beyond facilitating exchange?


 Because money determines wages Because changes in liquidity preference spill over into goods and asset markets Because money controls government budgets Because money is scarce




Hint

Changes in money demand spill over into spending and investment decisions.



AN7) Why is money’s role as Medium of Exchange insufficient on its own to guarantee efficient outcomes?


 Because prices may be regulated Because production may be limited Because coordination failures and liquidity hoarding can still occur Because money may depreciate




Hint

Even with money, hoarding and coordination failures can prevent efficient outcomes.



AN8) Why is liquidity described as both a property of assets and a property of the monetary system?


 Because central banks set liquidity Because liquidity depends on both asset characteristics and social acceptance Because liquidity is fixed over time Because liquidity is measurable in money units




Hint

Liquidity depends on asset features and on whether others accept it in exchange.



AN9) Why can an increase in the public’s desire for liquidity reduce aggregate demand?


 Because prices fall Because people substitute money for consumption and investment Because banks reduce lending Because wages fall




Hint

When people hold more money, they spend less, reducing aggregate demand.



AN10) Which of the following best captures the fundamental difference between Keynesian and Classical views of money?


 Keynes focuses on inflation; Classics focus on growth Keynes sees money as neutral; Classics do not Keynes emphasises coordination frictions; Classics assume they are negligible Keynes focuses on fiscal policy; Classics on monetary policy




Hint

The key difference is whether markets are assumed to coordinate automatically.
crumbs: Topic 1 - The Nature and Economic Role of Money

title: Topic 1 - MCQs Formative Assessment
text:
Problem Solving

PS1) Two traders meet: one has Apples and wants Bananas; the other has Bananas and wants Apples. What exchange friction is absent in this case?


 Search costs Misaligned preferences Double coincidence of wants Price uncertainty




Hint

When each trader wants what the other has, no matching friction arises.



PS2) Why does introducing money allow a trader to accept a good they do not want to consume?


 Because money increases utility directly Because money can be exchanged later for preferred goods Because money is scarce Because money stabilises prices




Hint

People accept money because it can later be exchanged for desired goods.



PS3) Three traders each prefer a good they do not own. Why does no bilateral trade take place under barter?


 Prices are unknown Preferences are cyclical and misaligned Goods are indivisible Endowments are unequal




Hint

If preferences form a cycle, no pairwise trade satisfies both parties.



PS4) Why might a trader refuse to act as a “middleman” by accepting their least-preferred good?


 Because it reduces total surplus Because they risk being unable to trade it away later Because it violates rationality Because it is illegal




Hint

Accepting an unwanted good is risky if it cannot be traded away later.



PS5) Which institutional arrangement could replicate the role of money in a small economy?


 A central warehouse Multilateral simultaneous exchange Government price fixing Interest-bearing accounts




Hint

Multilateral exchange can replicate money but only if everyone coordinates simultaneously.



PS6) Why does multilateral exchange become impractical as the number of traders increases?


 Because preferences become unstable Because coordinating many participants simultaneously becomes difficult Because prices cannot be calculated Because goods become scarce




Hint

The more participants, the harder it becomes to coordinate simultaneous exchange.



PS7) Suppose people suddenly fear future shortages and increase their money holdings. What immediate effect is most likely?


 Increased consumption Reduced spending on goods and assets Higher production Increased inflation




Hint

Holding more money means postponing consumption and investment.



PS8) Which scenario best illustrates a coordination failure rather than a technological failure?


 A factory cannot produce enough output Traders fail to exchange even though mutually beneficial trades exist A machine breaks down A resource becomes depleted




Hint

The problem is not production but failure to realise mutually beneficial trades.



PS9) Why can increased liquidity preference cause a recession even when productive capacity is unchanged?


 Because wages fall Because firms become less efficient Because spending declines, reducing aggregate demand Because inflation rises




Hint

Lower spending reduces output even if productive capacity is unchanged.



PS10) Which policy is most directly aimed at counteracting a surge in liquidity hoarding?


 Raising interest rates Cutting taxes Expanding the money supply or lowering interest rates Reducing government spending




Hint

Lower interest rates or higher money supply make holding money less attractive.
crumbs: Topic 1 - The Nature and Economic Role of Money

title: Topic 1 - MCQs Formative Assessment
text:
Mathematical Thinking

MT1) In an economy with 2 goods, how many bilateral exchange ratios are needed without a unit of account?


 1 2 3 4




Hint

With two goods, there is only one pairwise price ratio.



MT2) In an economy with 3 goods, how many bilateral exchange ratios are required without money?


 2 3 4 6




Hint

The number of ratios equals the number of distinct good pairs.



MT3) In an economy with 5 goods, how many bilateral exchange ratios are needed?


 5 10 15 20




Hint

Use the combinatorial formula for choosing pairs.



MT4) If the price of Apples is \(P_A = 0.5\) and the price of Bananas is \(P_B = 0.25\), what is the exchange ratio of Bananas per Apple?


 0.5 1 2 4




Hint

Exchange ratios are obtained by dividing one price by another.



MT5) If \(P_A = 2\) and \(P_B = 4\), what is the exchange ratio of Apples per Banana?


 0.25 0.5 2 4




Hint

“Apples per Banana” is the inverse of “Bananas per Apple.”



MT6) An economy has 10 goods. Approximately how many exchange ratios are required without a unit of account?


 10 25 45 100




Hint

The number of ratios grows with n², not linearly.



MT7) If the number of goods doubles from 50 to 100, by approximately what factor does the number of exchange ratios increase?


 It doubles It triples It quadruples It increases tenfold




Hint

Because ratios grow with n², doubling goods quadruples ratios.



MT8) Suppose there are 700 goods. Approximately how many exchange ratios exist without money?


 70,000 140,000 245,000 490,000




Hint

For large n, n(n−1)/2 is approximately n²/2.



MT9) If \(P_A/P_B = 2\) and \(P_B/P_C = 3\), what is \(P_A/P_C\)?


 1.5 2 5 6




Hint

To combine relative prices, multiply the ratios.

title: Monetary Economics
text:
Abstract. Money reduces the frictions of decentralised exchange by providing a unit of account, a medium of exchange, and a store of value. This note sets out those functions, illustrates why barter scales poorly, and connects liquidity, search frictions, and macro perspectives on money.



Money is a core institution of modern economies. A practical working definition is that money is any asset that is generally accepted as payment for goods and services in a given economic community. The defining feature here is general acceptability: an agent accepts money in exchange not because they wish to consume it, but because they expect others to accept it in subsequent transactions.
Money matters because it makes decentralised exchange feasible at scale. In a pure barter economy, trade requires a double coincidence of wants: each party must have what the other desires (Jevons, 1875/1876). This requirement is restrictive and generates significant transaction costs. Money relaxes this constraint by allowing exchange to occur in (at least) two steps: sell what you have for money, then use money to purchase what you want.
Historically, many objects have served monetary roles: commodity monies (e.g., gold and silver), representative monies (claims redeemable into a commodity), and, today, fiat money issued by the state and/or central bank. Modern fiat money is not redeemable for a commodity and is intrinsically worthless in consumption terms; its value is sustained by institutional frameworks, legal and tax structures, and credibility. In the contemporary economy, money exists in multiple forms: physical currency, bank deposits transferable through payment systems, and central-bank reserves used for interbank settlement.
This chapter is organised around the canonical functions of money:

Unit of account (the economy’s common measure of value),
Medium of exchange (the means of payment in transactions),
Store of value (an asset held over time).

We then analyse liquidity—the property that links money to broader asset markets—and conclude with the contrast between Classical and Keynesian perspectives on money’s macroeconomic importance (Keynes, 1936).




A unit of account is a common measure in which prices and values are expressed. This role is conceptually distinct from the medium-of-exchange role: a society could in principle use an abstract unit of account for pricing and contracting while settling transactions with other assets. In practice, however, the monetary unit (pounds, euros, dollars) typically serves as the unit of account.


The most fundamental object in valuation is the relative price (or exchange ratio): how many units of one good exchange for one unit of another.
Without a unit of account, describing values requires listing pairwise exchange ratios for all goods. The number of required exchange ratios grows quickly with the number of goods. With n goods, a complete barter price system requires \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) exchange ratios. For large n, this is approximately \(n^2/2\), which becomes unmanageable as product variety increases.
A unit of account dramatically reduces informational complexity. If each good has a money price, only n prices need to be quoted, and any relative price can be computed as a ratio of two money prices. This is the economy of measurement created by money as unit of account.



The unit-of-account function is most useful when the unit is relatively stable in purchasing power. If the unit itself changes value unpredictably, it is like trying to measure length with a ruler that keeps changing size. Inflation makes price comparisons harder, disrupts long-term contracting, and increases the resources devoted to repricing and indexation.
In high-inflation or hyperinflation episodes, domestic money often fails as a unit of account and people may shift to a foreign currency (partial “dollarisation”) or to indexed units. For example, Venezuela experienced extremely high inflation in the late 2010s, and pricing and saving behaviour increasingly moved toward stable foreign currencies (IMF DataMapper, n.d.). The general economic point is that price stability supports the unit-of-account role; instability undermines it.



Post‑2010 innovations highlight that being technologically novel is not sufficient to become a unit of account. Many cryptocurrencies are highly volatile, which makes them unattractive as pricing units for everyday goods and services. Even where legal experiments occurred—such as El Salvador’s 2021 Bitcoin legal tender policy—prices and contracts largely remained denominated in dollars, not Bitcoin, consistent with the idea that a unit of account requires stability and broad trust. IMF programme documentation reports that legal changes in 2025 removed key legal-tender features (including the obligation to accept Bitcoin), reflecting limited adoption and significant policy concerns (IMF, 2025).
By contrast, stablecoins seek to inherit stability by pegging to a fiat unit (usually the U.S. dollar). Their “moneyness” therefore depends on the credibility of the peg and on the legal/financial structures backing the promise of convertibility.





A medium of exchange is an asset that agents accept in exchange for goods and services with the intention of using it to purchase other goods and services in the future. This function is the most visible and is closely tied to money’s central economic contribution: reducing transaction costs.


Barter trade is a one-step exchange of one good for another. A monetary transaction typically involves two steps (sell for money, then buy with money), which may appear more complex at first glance. The key point is that barter requires a double coincidence of wants. In a decentralised economy with many goods and heterogeneous preferences, satisfying this condition is rare and costly.
Jevons (1875/1876) emphasised that the main friction is not conceptual but practical: it is costly to search for a counterparty who both has what you want and wants what you have. Monetary exchange solves this problem by allowing trade with any counterparty who accepts money, which—by definition—is “everyone.” ### A concrete example: three agents and three goods {#three-agents-example}
To illustrate the problem of the double coincidence of wants, consider three traders and three goods:

Harriet has 6 Bananas; she prefers: Bananas (6) ≻ Apples (3) ≻ Cabbage (1)
Ina has 1 Cabbage; she prefers: Cabbage (1) ≻ Bananas (6) ≻ Apples (3)
Jamal has 3 Apples; he prefers: Apples (3) ≻ Cabbage (1) ≻ Bananas (6)

Each trader ends up with their least preferred good. Under pure barter, achieving mutual benefit is complicated:

Harriet wants to trade her Bananas for Apples (Jamal’s good), but Jamal wants to trade his Apples for Cabbage (Ina’s good), not Bananas.
Ina wants to trade her Cabbage for Bananas (Harriet’s good), but Harriet wants Apples, not Cabbage.

Without a medium of exchange, all three traders would need to coordinate a multilateral trade: Harriet gives Bananas to Ina, Jamal gives Apples to Harriet, and Ina gives Cabbage to Jamal—all simultaneously. This requires perfect knowledge of each other’s preferences and strict temporal coordination.
With a widely accepted medium of exchange (money), the problem vanishes: each trader sells their current good for money, then uses money to purchase their preferred good. Transaction costs are dramatically reduced, and agents can trade independently rather than relying on simultaneous trilateral coordination. ### Trading posts, market structure, and the economy of exchange
A useful way to see the role of a medium of exchange is to imagine that, without money, an economy would require a dense network of “trading posts” or market arrangements for each pair of goods. With n goods, \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) bilateral trading posts would be needed for direct barter across all pairs, which scales poorly. With money as a medium of exchange, each good needs only a market against money, and any two goods can be traded indirectly through money. This is the economy of exchange that money provides.



Modern monetary economics formalised these intuitions in search-theoretic models. In seminal work, Kiyotaki and Wright (1989) show that under trading frictions, certain assets can become accepted as media of exchange because they lower transaction costs and increase the probability of successful trade. Later work (Kiyotaki & Wright, 1993) provides a broader framework for monetary exchange as a solution to decentralised trading problems.
These models help clarify why acceptability is both cause and consequence of being money: an asset is accepted because others accept it, creating a network effect. But acceptance is not arbitrary; assets with suitable properties (portability, durability, divisibility, and low verification cost) are more likely to emerge as media of exchange.



In modern economies, many transactions are executed electronically. Cards, mobile wallets, and real-time transfer systems are payment technologies layered on top of money. Under the hood, settlement typically occurs in central bank money (reserves and cash) and bank deposit money denominated in the national unit of account.
Cryptocurrencies have been proposed as alternative payment instruments. Empirical work suggests that, in many jurisdictions, their use as everyday payment media has been limited (Umlauft, 2018). Where adoption has been attempted at national scale, the outcomes underline the importance of stability, infrastructure, regulation, and trust.





Money also functions as a store of value: it transfers purchasing power through time. This function follows naturally from the medium-of-exchange role because sales and purchases are often separated by time; in that gap, money is held as an asset.
However, money is not the only store of value. Bonds, equities, property, and other assets store value and often deliver higher returns. Money’s comparative advantage is liquidity—the capacity to be used immediately as a means of payment.


Because money typically yields little or no interest, holding money involves an opportunity cost: the foregone return from holding an interest-bearing asset instead. This opportunity cost is a key determinant of money demand.
Keynes (1936) emphasised that agents demand money not only for transactions but also for liquidity as a store of value under uncertainty. In this framework, the interest rate can be interpreted as a premium required to induce agents to hold less liquid assets instead of money.



Inflation erodes the real value of nominal money balances. Over long horizons, cash is typically a poor store of value unless nominal interest on liquid balances compensates for inflation. When inflation is high and unpredictable, agents shift into alternative stores of value (foreign currency, real assets, indexed claims), weakening money’s store-of-value role and potentially destabilising the monetary system.
Recent macroeconomic experience renewed attention to these issues. Following the COVID‑19 shock, several advanced economies experienced the highest inflation rates in decades. A large empirical literature examines the roles of supply constraints, fiscal expansion, and monetary conditions; as part of this debate, BIS research has argued that money growth helps explain cross-country variation in the inflation surge, especially when inflation moves into higher regimes (Borio, Hofmann, & Zakrajšek, 2023; Borio, Hofmann, & Zakrajšek, 2024).





Liquidity is a central concept linking money to asset markets and financial stability. A practical definition is:

Liquidity is the ease with which an asset can be exchanged for goods and services (or converted into a generally accepted means of payment) quickly, predictably, and with little loss of value.

Money is the most liquid asset. Other assets are “money-like” to the extent that they can be converted into money rapidly at low cost and low risk.


Liquidity is commonly associated with:

Marketability (active markets and many potential buyers),
Predictability of exchange value (low short-run price volatility),
Reversibility (small bid–ask spreads and low transaction costs),
Divisibility (capacity to trade in small denominations).

These criteria help explain why agents are often willing to hold money despite its low return: they obtain liquidity services in exchange for foregoing interest.



Because liquidity is a spectrum, monetary authorities define multiple monetary aggregates. Narrow measures (e.g., currency and demand deposits) are most liquid. Broader measures include less liquid but still money-like instruments (e.g., some savings deposits).
In the U.S., widely used series include M2, available through the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis FRED database (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, n.d.). While definitions differ across countries, the central idea is consistent: as aggregates broaden, liquidity declines and return often increases.



Liquidity conditions can change abruptly in crises. Even normally liquid markets can become illiquid when risk aversion spikes and balance sheets are constrained, producing a “flight to liquidity.” This is one reason central banks maintain lender-of-last-resort frameworks and market backstops to prevent liquidity shocks from turning into solvency crises and macroeconomic contractions.



CBDCs are frequently analysed as potential new forms of sovereign money, designed to be safe and highly liquid. The Atlantic Council’s CBDC Tracker reports that a large share of countries are exploring, piloting, or developing CBDCs (Atlantic Council, n.d.). If introduced at scale, CBDCs could reshape retail payments, alter the composition of liquid assets held by households, and raise new questions for banking-sector funding and financial stability.





The macroeconomic importance of money is often introduced through a contrast between Classical and Keynesian approaches.


In classical monetary thought, money is essential for transactions but largely neutral in the long run: changes in the money supply affect nominal variables (such as prices) but not real variables (such as output and employment), once prices fully adjust. This idea underpins the classical dichotomy and long-run neutrality propositions often associated with quantity-theoretic reasoning.



Keynes argued that money is not only a medium of exchange and unit of account; it is also a store of value held for liquidity under uncertainty (Keynes, 1936). Because agents can choose to hoard money, shifts in liquidity preference can spill over into asset markets and goods markets, affecting interest rates, investment, and aggregate demand. Under price and wage rigidities, these monetary and financial conditions can affect real output and employment in the short and medium run.



Contemporary macroeconomics typically combines elements of both traditions: money is often viewed as approximately neutral in the long run, but monetary policy and liquidity conditions are central to short-run fluctuations. Modern frameworks often focus on interest rates and financial conditions rather than money aggregates alone (e.g., Woodford, 2003), but the post‑pandemic inflation episode revived interest in money growth and liquidity alongside standard policy-rate channels (Borio et al., 2023; 2024).

In what sense is a stable unit of account a public good? How does inflation undermine it?
Using the idea of opportunity cost, explain why higher nominal interest rates typically reduce desired money holdings.
Why might a technologically superior payment instrument fail as “money” if it lacks broad acceptability?
How could CBDCs change the composition of liquid assets held by households and the banking sector?

title: Topic 2 - Indicative Answers
text:
Question: Consider a trader with utility function \(U = d_1^{\alpha} d_2^{1-\alpha}\) where \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) are demands for goods 1 and 2, and \(\alpha \in (0,1)\). Initial endowment: \(s_1, s_2\) units.

Write an expression for her nominal income \(y_N\) given prices \(P_1\) and \(P_2\).
Write her budget constraint.
Write down the utility maximisation problem and derive first-order conditions.
Solve for demands \(d_1, d_2\) as functions of \(P_1, P_2\), and \(y_N\).
Express demands as functions of \(P_1, P_2, s_1, s_2\). What happens if all prices double?
Calculate net purchase with \(s_1=2, s_2=10, P_1=2, P_2=1, \alpha=0.5\).



(a) Nominal income: \(y_N = P_1 s_1 + P_2 s_2\)
(b) Budget constraint: \(P_1 d_1 + P_2 d_2 = y_N\)
(c) Utility maximisation problem using Lagrangian: \[L = d_1^\alpha d_2^{(1-\alpha)} + \lambda[y_N - P_1 d_1 - P_2 d_2]\]
First-order conditions: \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial d_1} = \alpha\left(\frac{d_2}{d_1}\right)^{(1-\alpha)} - \lambda P_1 = 0\] \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial d_2} = (1-\alpha)\left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^\alpha - \lambda P_2 = 0\] \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial \lambda} = y_N - P_1 d_1 - P_2 d_2 = 0\]
(d) Combining FOCs yields: \[d_1^* = \alpha\left(\frac{y_N}{P_1}\right)\] \[d_2^* = (1-\alpha)\left(\frac{y_N}{P_2}\right)\]
These represent optimal choices (demands).
(e) Expanding \(y_N\): \[d_1^* = \alpha\left[s_1 + \frac{P_2}{P_1}s_2\right]\] \[d_2^* = (1-\alpha)\left[\frac{P_1}{P_2}s_1 + s_2\right]\]
If all prices double, the ratios \(P_1/P_2\) and \(P_2/P_1\) are unaffected, so demands remain unchanged. This reflects the homogeneity of demand functions.
(f) With \(s_1=2\), \(s_2=10\), \(P_1=2\), \(P_2=1\), \(\alpha=0.5\): \[d_1^* = 0.5\left[2 + \frac{1}{2}(10)\right] = 3.5\] \[d_2^* = 0.5\left[\frac{2}{1}(2) + 10\right] = 7\]
Net purchase: \[d_1^* - s_1 = 3.5 - 2 = 1.5 \text{ (net purchase of good 1)}\] \[d_2^* - s_2 = 7 - 10 = -3 \text{ (net sale of good 2)}\]
Note that net purchase of 1 = net sale of 2 in value terms.

Calculate net purchase with \(s_1=2, s_2=10, P_1=2, P_2=1, \alpha=0.5\).



(a) Nominal income: \(y_N = P_1 s_1 + P_2 s_2\)
(b) Budget constraint: \(P_1 d_1 + P_2 d_2 = y_N\)
(c) Utility maximisation problem using Lagrangian: \[L = d_1^\alpha d_2^{(1-\alpha)} + \lambda[y_N - P_1 d_1 - P_2 d_2]\]
First-order conditions: \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial d_1} = \alpha\left(\frac{d_2}{d_1}\right)^{(1-\alpha)} - \lambda P_1 = 0\] \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial d_2} = (1-\alpha)\left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^\alpha - \lambda P_2 = 0\] \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial \lambda} = y_N - P_1 d_1 - P_2 d_2 = 0\]
(d) Combining FOCs yields: \[d_1^* = \alpha\left(\frac{y_N}{P_1}\right)\] \[d_2^* = (1-\alpha)\left(\frac{y_N}{P_2}\right)\]
These represent optimal choices (demands).
(e) Expanding \(y_N\): \[d_1^* = \alpha\left[s_1 + \frac{P_2}{P_1}s_2\right]\] \[d_2^* = (1-\alpha)\left[\frac{P_1}{P_2}s_1 + s_2\right]\]
If all prices double, the ratios \(P_1/P_2\) and \(P_2/P_1\) are unaffected, so demands remain unchanged. This reflects the homogeneity of demand functions.
(f) With \(s_1=2\), \(s_2=10\), \(P_1=2\), \(P_2=1\), \(\alpha=0.5\): \[d_1^* = 0.5\left[2 + \frac{1}{2}(10)\right] = 3.5\] \[d_2^* = 0.5\left[\frac{2}{1}(2) + 10\right] = 7\]
Net purchase: \[d_1^* - s_1 = 3.5 - 2 = 1.5 \text{ (net purchase of good 1)}\] \[d_2^* - s_2 = 7 - 10 = -3 \text{ (net sale of good 2)}\]
Note that net purchase of 1 = net sale of 2 in value terms.

title: Topic 2 - Indicative Answers
section: Question 2: General Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
text:
Question 2: General Equilibrium in an Exchange Economy
Question: Consider 2 traders (A, B) and 2 goods (1, 2) with prices \(P_1, P_2\). Endowments: \(s^A = (s_1^A, s_2^A)\), \(s^B = (s_1^B, s_2^B)\).

Write each agent’s budget constraint in (i) nominal terms and (ii) real terms using good 1 as numeraire.
Write the market clearing condition for each good.
Show that when (i) budget constraints bind and (ii) market 1 clears, then market 2 must also clear. What ‘law’ is illustrated?


Indicative Answer
(a) Budget constraints:
Nominal terms: \[\text{Agent A: } P_1 d_1^{A*} + P_2 d_2^{A*} \leq P_1 s_1^A + P_2 s_2^A\] \[\text{Agent B: } P_1 d_1^{B*} + P_2 d_2^{B*} \leq P_1 s_1^B + P_2 s_2^B\]
Real terms (good 1 as numeraire): \[\text{Agent A: } d_1^{A*} + \frac{P_2}{P_1}d_2^{A*} \leq s_1^A + \frac{P_2}{P_1}s_2^A\] \[\text{Agent B: } d_1^{B*} + \frac{P_2}{P_1}d_2^{B*} \leq s_1^B + \frac{P_2}{P_1}s_2^B\]
where demands are functions of relative price and real income.
(b) Market clearing conditions: \[\text{Good 1: } d_1^{A*} + d_1^{B*} = s_1^A + s_1^B \rightarrow D_1 = S_1\] \[\text{Good 2: } d_2^{A*} + d_2^{B*} = s_2^A + s_2^B \rightarrow D_2 = S_2\]
(c) Suppose \(D_1 = S_1\) (good 1 market clears) and budget constraints bind (hold as “=”).
Adding both agents’ real budget constraints: \[d_1^{A*} + \frac{P_2}{P_1}d_2^{A*} + d_1^{B*} + \frac{P_2}{P_1}d_2^{B*} = s_1^A + \frac{P_2}{P_1}s_2^A + s_1^B + \frac{P_2}{P_1}s_2^B\]
Rearranging: \[(d_1^{A*} + d_1^{B*}) + \frac{P_2}{P_1}(d_2^{A*} + d_2^{B*}) = (s_1^A + s_1^B) + \frac{P_2}{P_1}(s_2^A + s_2^B)\]
Since \(D_1 = S_1\), the terms in first brackets cancel: \[\frac{P_2}{P_1}(d_2^{A*} + d_2^{B*}) = \frac{P_2}{P_1}(s_2^A + s_2^B)\] Therefore: \(D_2 = S_2\)
This establishes Walras’ Law: If n-1 markets clear and all budget constraints bind, the nth market must also clear.

title: Topic 2 - MCQs Formative Assessment
text:
How to use this quiz



This quiz is designed as a formative self-assessment tool, not as a test.
Its purpose is to help you: - check your understanding of the key concepts from Topic 2, - identify which types of thinking you find more difficult, and - guide your revision before the tutorial and future assessments.


Each question belongs to one of four categories:

Subject Knowledge (SK): definitions, concepts, and facts.

Analysis (AN): understanding relationships and economic mechanisms.

Problem Solving (PS): applying concepts to new situations.

Mathematical Thinking (MT): working with ratios, prices, and scaling.

Your score will be broken down by category so you can see where you are strong and where you need more practice.




You may use your notes and the lecture materials.
Take your time — the goal is understanding, not speed.
Use the Hints if you get stuck.
You may refresh and retry the quiz as many times as you like.





A low score is not a problem — it tells you what to focus on.
If you score low in:

SK: revise definitions and core concepts.
AN: revisit the logic of the models and examples.
PS: practise applying concepts to new cases.
MT: practise the price and ratio calculations.





The leaderboard is optional and anonymous. It exists only to make practice more engaging.
It has no effect on your grade and is not used for evaluation.
The only purpose of this quiz is to support your learning.
